Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 1:

(p-84) Surat al-Naba' is Meccan, and its verses number forty.

﴿Amma﴾ Its original form is (ʿammā), from which the alif was dropped, either to distinguish the interrogative "mā" from other uses, or intentionally for lightness because of its frequent use. It has also been read in its original form (ʿammā). The indefiniteness of "mā" here serves to signal the great magnitude of the thing asked about, its awesomeness, and its being beyond the familiar categories of kinds; that is, "about some tremendously important matter."

﴿They ask one another﴾ That is, the people of Mecca. They used to ask one another about the Resurrection (al-baʿth) and discuss it among themselves, in denial and mockery. However, they did not ask in the manner of inquiring about its reality (ḥaqīqah) and essence (musammā), but about its occurrence, which is one of its states (ḥāl) and one of its attributes (waṣf). For although "mā" is placed to seek the realities of things and the referents of their names, as in your saying: "What is the angel?" and "What is the spirit?", it may also be used to seek the attribute and the state. You say: "What is Zayd?" and it is answered: "A scholar," or "A physician." It has also been said: they were asking the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers about it in mockery, like their saying: "they call them" (yatadāʿawnahum), meaning "they call them" (yadʿūnahum). The verification of this is that the form (ṣīghah) of tafāʿul in transitive verbs is set to express that the action proceeds from multiple parties and falls upon them, such that each one becomes both agent and object at once. But it is raised by attributing the verb to it, giving preference to its agency, and its objecthood is left to be understood by the intellect, as in your saying: "tarāʾā al-qawm," meaning each of them saw the other. It may also be stripped of the second meaning, so that it signifies merely the action proceeding from multiple parties, without considering its falling upon them; then the verb takes a multiple object, as in the example mentioned, or a single object, as in your saying: "tarāʾawā al-hilāl." It may also be elided when it is evident, as in the case we are dealing with. So the meaning is: "About what are these people asking the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers?!" Sometimes it is also stripped of the proceeding of the action from multiple parties, so that it signifies the multiplicity of its object with the unity of the agent, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ and the saying of the Exalted:

﴿About the great news﴾ is an explanation of the matter being asked about, placed after its magnification by leaving its affair vague and directing the listeners' minds toward it, treating them as though they were inquirers. Presenting it in the form of a question from the Knower of the Unseen serves as an alert that, because its counterpart is cut off and its like does not exist, it lies outside the sphere of creatures' knowledge. It is fitting that its knowledge be sought and that one ask about it. It is as if it were said: "About what are they asking? Shall I inform you of it?" Then it was said, by way of answer, "about the great news," following the pattern of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ (p-85) ﴿It is for God, the One, the Subduer.﴾ So "ʿan" (about) is connected to what is indicated by the mentioned element, namely a implied element that should be supposed after it, in haste toward the explanation and in observance of the order of the question. This is the one that befits the sublime eloquence of the revelation. It has also been said that it is connected to the mentioned element, and that "ʿamma" (about what) is connected to an implied element that it explains. This is supported by the fact that it was read as ﴿ʿammahu﴾. The more apparent view is that this is built on treating the connection as if it were a pause. It has been said that the first "ʿan" is for causation, as if it were said: "Why are they asking about the great news?" It has also been said, before the second "ʿan," that there is an implied interrogative, as if it were said: "About what are they asking, about the great news?" And "al-nabaʾ" (the news) is the report that has importance and weight. It has been described by His words, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 3:

﴿Concerning which they are in disagreement.﴾ This comes after the description of it as "the great" (al-'azim), as an emphasis on its gravity following another emphasis, and as an indication that the matter on which the questioning revolves is this one. "Fihi" (concerning it) is connected to "mukhtalifun" (in disagreement) and was placed before it out of concern for it and for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil). Making the relative clause a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) indicates permanence, meaning: they are firmly established in disagreement concerning it. So, from among them is the one who, certain of its impossibility, says:

"There is naught but our life of this world: we die and we live, and nothing destroys us but time. And we are not to be resurrected."

And from among them is the doubter who says:

"We know not what the Hour is. We only suppose a supposition, and we are not certain."

It has been said: among them are those who deny both resurrections (al-ma'adayn) together, like these, and among them are those who deny only the bodily resurrection (al-ma'ad al-jismani), like the majority of the Christians. The disagreement has also been taken to mean a disagreement over the manner of the denial: among them are those who deny it because they deny the Maker who chooses (al-Sani' al-Mukhtar), and among them are those who deny it on the basis of the impossibility of re-creating what has ceased to exist in its very same individual form. Taking it to mean disagreement in negation and affirmation, on the basis of generalizing the questioning to both groups, the Muslims and the disbelievers, so that the questioning of the first group is to increase them in fear and readiness, and the questioning of the latter group is to increase them in disbelief and obstinacy, is refuted by His, the Exalted's, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 4:

﴿Nay, they will come to know!﴾ ... etc. This is clear evidence that what is meant is the disagreement of those who are ignorant of it and deny it; for the rebuke and the threat revolve around this, not around the disagreement of the believers with them. Restricting the two (the rebuke and the threat) to the disbelievers, on the basis of restricting the pronoun in "they will come to know" to them, despite the generality of the two preceding pronouns to all, is something from which the revelation ought to be kept free. This is what sound reflection has led to. What verification requires and careful consideration demands is that their disagreement be understood as their opposition to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, such that what is considered in the disagreement is the mere occurrence of the act from more than one party, as was mentioned in the question. For the form ifti'al (iftaʿala) and the form tafa'ul (tafāʿul) are sister forms, like istibaq (racing) and tasabuq (racing one another), and intidal (shooting arrows at one another) and tanadul (shooting one another), and so on; whatever applies to one of them applies to the other, not in the sense of some of them opposing others from both sides. For although all of them deserve the rebuke and the threat, the deserving of each side of them is not because of its opposition to the other side, since there is no correctness in any of them such that whoever opposes it would deserve blame; rather it is because of their opposition to him, peace and blessings be upon him. So "Nay" is a rebuke to them against questioning and disagreeing in the two senses mentioned, and "they will come to know" is a threat to them by way of resumption (istiʾnaf) and a reason for the rebuke. The sin (in sa-yaʿlamūna) is for proximity and emphasis, and its object is not what the context indicates of the occurrence of that about which they question, and the occurrence of that about which they disagree, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not raise up those who die﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that He may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾, the verse. For that is devoid of explicit threat; rather it is an expression of the various calamities and punishments they will encounter. And the expression of meeting them by "knowledge" (p-86) is because it occurs in the context of questioning and disagreement. The meaning is: that they may desist from what they are upon, for they will soon come to know the reality of the situation when punishment and retribution befall them. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 5:

﴿Then no! They will come to know.﴾ It is a repetition of the rebuke and the warning, for the sake of emphasis and intensification of the affirmation and stress. The "thumma" (then) indicates that the second warning is more eloquent and more severe. It has been said: the first is at the time of death-agony (al-naz'), and the second is on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: the first is for the Resurrection (al-ba'th), and the second is for the recompense (al-jaza'). It is also read as "sa-ta'lamun" with the ta' (second person), in the manner of iltifat (shift) to direct address, in agreement with the direct addresses that follow it, to intensify the rebuke and the warning. This is not on the assumption of an implied "Say to them" (qul lahum), as has been imagined, for that would involve a disruption of the eloquent coherence of the noble composition, which is not hidden. And His, exalted be He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verses 6–7:

﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle?﴾ ﴿And the mountains as pegs?﴾ ... etc. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought forward to confirm the Great News (al-naba') about which they were asking, by enumerating some of the evident proofs of its reality, after having alerted to them through the rebuke and threat mentioned. From here it becomes clear that what they were asking about is the Resurrection (al-ba'th), not the Qur'an or the prophethood of the Prophet (peace be upon him), as has been said. The hamza (of interrogation, alif-hamza) is for affirmation (taqrir), and the shift to address (iltifat ila al-khitab) in the well-known reading is for emphasis in imposing obligation and rebuke. Al-mihad means the spread-out surface and the bedding. It was also read as mahdan (مَهْدًا), likening it to the cradle of a child (mahd al-sabi), which is what is prepared for him so that he is laid down upon it; this is a designation of the thing made into a cradle by its verbal noun (tasmiyat al-mamhud bi-al-masdar). Making the mountains pegs for it means their being fixed in it, just as a tent is fixed by pegs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verses 6–7:

﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle?﴾ ﴿And the mountains as pegs?﴾ ... etc. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought forward to confirm the Great News (al-naba') about which they were asking, by enumerating some of the evident proofs of its reality, after having alerted to them through the rebuke and threat mentioned. From here it becomes clear that what they were asking about is the Resurrection (al-ba'th), not the Qur'an or the prophethood of the Prophet (peace be upon him), as has been said. The hamza (of interrogation, alif-hamza) is for affirmation (taqrir), and the shift to address (iltifat ila al-khitab) in the well-known reading is for emphasis in imposing obligation and rebuke. Al-mihad means the spread-out surface and the bedding. It was also read as mahdan (مَهْدًا), likening it to the cradle of a child (mahd al-sabi), which is what is prepared for him so that he is laid down upon it; this is a designation of the thing made into a cradle by its verbal noun (tasmiyat al-mamhud bi-al-masdar). Making the mountains pegs for it means their being fixed in it, just as a tent is fixed by pegs.

**﴿And We created you﴾** is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the negated imperfect verb (*muḍāriʿ*) that is introduced by **لَمْ** (*lam*), and it falls under the same ruling, since it carries the meaning of **أَمَا جَعَلْنَا** (*ʾa-lam najʿal*, "Did We not make...?") and so on. Alternatively, it is coordinated with what the rhetorical denial (*al-inkār al-taqrīrī*) requires, since it carries the meaning of saying: "Indeed We have made...", and so on.

**﴿Pairs﴾** means kinds: male and female, so that each of the two kinds may find tranquility in the other, the affairs of companionship and livelihood may be ordered, and procreation may be made possible.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 9:

﴿And We made your sleep a subat (repose)﴾. That is: death. For it is one of the two kinds of taking (tawaffi), because of the complete sharing between them in the cessation of the rulings of life. Upon this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night﴾, and the saying of the Exalted: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep﴾. It was also said: a cutting off from sensation and movement, to give ease to the animal faculties and to remove their fatigue. The first is the one fitting to the context, as you will come to know.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 10:

﴿And We made the night﴾ — that in which sleep generally occurs.

﴿a garment﴾ — it covers you with its darkness as clothing covers you. Perhaps what is meant by it is what one is covered with during sleep, such as a blanket (lihaf) or the like, for the resemblance of the night to it is more complete, and its consideration in achieving the purpose is more inclusive. Thus He made the night a place for sleep, which is made a kind of death, just as He made the day a place for wakefulness (p-87), which is expressed by life in His saying, may He be exalted:

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 11:

﴿And We made the day a time of livelihood﴾. That is: a time of life, in which you are raised up from your sleep, which is the brother of death, as in His saying, exalted is He: "And it is He who made the night a garment for you, and sleep a rest, and made the day a resurrection" (Qur'an 25:47). Making the night a garment is a metaphor for its concealing you from the eyes of one who wishes to flee from an enemy, or to raid him by night, or the like, which has no relevance to the context. Likewise, making the day a time of moving about in seeking livelihoods and needs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 12:

﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾. That is: seven heavens, strong in their creation and firm in their construction, upon which the passage of ages and the revolution of eras has no effect. The expression of their creation by "building" is based on treating them as the domes erected over creation. The placing of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf, "above you") before the object (al-maf'ul, "seven strong [heavens]") is not merely for the sake of observing the rhyme (al-fawasil, the verse-endings), but to create suspense (al-tashwiq) toward it: for that which by rights should come first, when it is delayed, leaves the soul awaiting it, and when it then arrives, it settles in the soul with far greater firmness.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 13:**

﴿And We have made a blazing lamp.﴾ This *ja'l* (making, appointing) has the sense of *inshā'* (bringing into being) and *ibdā'* (originating), like *khalq* (creating), except that it is specific to creative bringing into being (*inshā' takwīnī*, creation by way of existence). It also carries the sense of *taqdīr* (determining) and *taswiyya* (fashioning in due proportion). This is general in its application, as in the noble verse, and it also applies to legislative making (*tashrī'ī*), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God did not make (*mā ja'ala Allāh*) any bahīra (a she-camel released from labour)﴾ ... and so on. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For each of you We have made (*ja'alnā*) a law (*shir'a*) and a way (*minhāj*)﴾.

Whatever the case, it indicates that its object (*maf'ūl*) is connected to something else, such that there is in it, or for it, or from it, or something similar, a valid connection (*mulābasa muṣaḥḥaḥa*). This is achieved by some adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*) coming between the two, whether it is *lāghw* (a dispensable phrase, in the sense of a non-essential adverbial) or *mustaqarr* (a phrase with an implied stative verb, such as "being in" or "being for"). However, this is not in the sense that it is a principal element of the sentence (*'umda*), but rather a qualifier (*qayd*) within it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He made between them a barrier (*barzakh*)﴾, and His saying: ﴿And He made in it firm mountains (*rawāsī*)﴾, and His saying: ﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a protector (*waliyy*)﴾, and the verse. Each of these adverbial phrases is either connected to the act of *ja'l* itself, or to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of its object, having been placed before it because the object is indefinite (*nakira*). In any case, it is a qualifier within the sentence. Even when the context requires that it be a principal element, the verb *ja'l* is then transitive to two objects, the second being the complement, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾. The matter may sometimes be confused, so that one supposes it to be a principal element, when in reality it is a qualifier in one of the two respects, as has passed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I am making (*jā'il*) a successor (*khalīfa*) on the earth﴾.

*Wahhāj* means blazing, burning intensely, shining brightly, from *wahajat al-nār* when the fire gave light, or it means reaching the utmost in heat, from *al-wahj*. What is intended by it is the sun. The expression of it as a lamp (*sirāj*) is among the parallel expressions to the expression of the creation of the heavens as a building (*binā'*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 14:

﴿And We sent down from the squeezing clouds﴾ (al-mu'sirat) are the clouds when they are about to squeeze out (rain), that is, they draw near to the point where the winds squeeze them so that they rain, just as in "uhsida al-zar'u" (the crop was harvested), when it is time for it to be harvested. From this comes "u'sirat al-jariyah" (the girl drew near to menstruating), when she is close to menstruating. Or (al-mu'sirat means) the winds, for which it is time to squeeze the clouds. It was recited as (bil-mu'sirat). The reasoning for this is that the sending down, wherever it comes from the squeezing ones, whether they are meant as clouds or winds, is done by them, as one says: "a'taahu min yadihi wa-biyadihi" (he gave it to him from his hand and by his hand). Al-mu'sirat has also been explained as the winds that possess whirlwinds (dhawat al-a'asir). Its basis is that the winds are the ones that (p-88) produce the clouds and cause their udders to flow, so they are suitable to be made the starting point of the sending down.

﴿abundant water﴾ meaning poured out in abundance. It is said: "thajja al-ma'u," meaning the water flowed abundantly, and "thajjahu," meaning he caused it to flow. From this is his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "The best of the Hajj is al-'ajj and al-thajj," meaning raising the voice with the talbiyah and pouring out the blood of the sacrificial animal. It was recited as (thajjaohan) with a ha' after the jim; they said: "mathajih al-ma'i" means its outlets (places where water pours out).

﴿That We may bring forth thereby﴾ by that water.

﴿grain﴾ that is used for food, like wheat, barley, and the like.

﴿and plants﴾ that is used for fodder, like chaff and herbage. The placing of grain first, although it comes after plants in the bringing forth, is due to its primacy and nobility, since most of it is the sustenance of humans.

﴿And gardens﴾. The word jannah (garden) originally refers to a single instance of the verbal noun of *janna*, meaning "he covered it," that is, concealed it. It is applied to palm trees and dense trees whose branches are interwoven so that they cast shade. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

*As if my two eyes, at the two buckets of a water-wheel of water-skins, were watering a remote garden (suhuqan).*

It is also applied to land that has trees. Al-Farra' said: "The jannah is that which contains palm trees, and the firdaws is that which contains vines, and the first is what is meant." His saying, exalted be He, ﴿ألفافًا﴾ (intertwined), means: densely entwined, some of them merged into others. They said: it has no singular, like *al-awza'* and *al-akhyaf* (which have no singular forms). It was said: its singular is *laff*, like *kinn* and *aknan* (shelter and shelters), or *lafif*, like *sharif* and *ashraf* (noble and nobles). It was said: it is the plural of *laff*, which is itself the plural of *laffa'*, like *khadir* and *khadra'* (green and green things). It was said: it is the plural of *multaffa* (intertwined), with the extra letters removed.

Know that the acts of His, glorified and exalted be He, that have been mentioned indicate the truth of the resurrection and its reality in three respects.

First: in terms of His power, exalted be He. Whoever is able to bring these wondrous acts into being without any pattern to imitate or any law to follow is more able and more powerful to bring about a return.

Second: in terms of His knowledge and wisdom. Whoever has produced these creations in a splendid design, leading to noble ends and beautiful benefits that return to creation, is impossible to deprive of these benefits entirely, or to fail to give them a lasting outcome.

Third: in terms of the act itself. Waking after sleep is a model of resurrection after death, which they witness every day. Likewise, the bringing forth of grain and plants from dead earth, which they behold at all times. It is as if it were said: Did We not perform these acts, both those of the horizons and those of the self, which indicate by various kinds of indication the truth of the resurrection, which necessitates belief in it? So why do you plunge into it in denial, and question one another about it in mockery?! And His saying, exalted be He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time.﴾ This begins an explanation of the secret behind delaying what they ask about and hasten for, saying: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" It is also a kind of detailed account of how it will occur and of the various kinds of punishment they will encounter at that time, in accordance with what the threat had stated in summary. That is: the Day of the Separation (fasl) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, between the creatures was, in His knowledge and decree, an appointed time and a fixed term for the resurrection of the first and the last, and for what follows from it of recompense, reward and punishment; it cannot be advanced or delayed beyond it. It has also been said: it is a limit by which the world is timed and ends, or a limit for the creatures at which they come to their end. There is no doubt that both of these are far from the closeness alluded to, given that the world ends at the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula). (p-89) And His saying, exalted is He:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 18:**

﴿On the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. That is, a second blast. It is either a substitute (*badal*) for "the Day of Judgement" (*yawm al-fasl*), or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*, a noun that clarifies the one before it) that serves to magnify and intensify its awe. There is no difficulty in the Judgement (*al-fasl*) being later than the blast, since it is an extended period: at its beginning comes the blast, and in the rest of it come the Judgement, its initial stages and its effects. The Trumpet (*al-sur*) is the horn into which Israfil (peace be upon him) will blow.

On the authority of Abu Hurayra (may God be pleased with him), that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When God, exalted is He, finished creating the heavens and the earth, He created the Trumpet and gave it to Israfil. He is holding it, placing it at his mouth, his gaze fixed on the Throne, awaiting the moment he is commanded, and then he will blow into it a blast after which none will remain alive except those whom God, exalted is He, wills." That is His saying: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills﴾. Then he will be commanded to blow another blast, and he will blow it, and no one dead will remain except that they will be raised and stand up. That is His saying: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾. The "fa" (then) in His saying ﴿so you will come﴾ is an eloquent *fa* (*fa fasiha*), which makes explicit an omitted clause, the omission being relied upon because the context indicates it, and to signal the extreme speed of the coming. It is like His saying: "We said: Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted," meaning: you will be raised from your graves, and then you will come to the place of standing (*al-mawqif*) immediately after that, without any delay at all.

﴿In throngs﴾: that is, in nations, each nation with its leader, as in His saying: "On the day We call every people by their leader." Or they will be in groups and companies, differing in their conditions and diverse in their states, according to the differences and variety of their deeds.

On the authority of Mu'adh (may God be pleased with him), that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) said: "O Mu'adh, you have asked about a grave matter among the matters," then he let his eyes flow with tears and said: "Ten categories of my community will be gathered: some of them in the form of monkeys, some of them in the form of pigs, some of them upside down with their feet above their faces, dragged upon them; some of them blind; some of them deaf and dumb; some of them chewing their tongues, which hang down upon their chests, with pus flowing from their mouths, which the people of the gathering find disgusting; some of them with their hands and feet cut off; some of them crucified on trunks of fire; some of them more foul-smelling than carrion; and some of them wearing flowing robes of tar, sticking to their skins. As for those in the form of monkeys, they are the tale-bearers among people. As for those in the form of pigs, they are the consumers of illicit gain (*ahl al-suht*). As for those upside down on their faces, they are the consumers of usury. As for the blind, they are those who are unjust in judgement. As for the deaf and dumb, they are those who are self-admiring in their deeds. As for those who chew their tongues, they are the scholars whose words contradicted their deeds. As for those whose hands and feet are cut off, they are those who harm their neighbours. As for those crucified on trunks of fire, they are the informers against people to the authorities. As for those more foul-smelling than carrion, they are those who pursue lusts and pleasures and withhold God's right in their wealth. As for those who wear the robes, they are the people of pride, boasting and arrogance."

"And the sky will be opened" — this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "yunfakh" (it will be blown into), and the use of the past form (ṣīghat al-māḍī) indicates certainty (li-l-dalālah ʿalā al-taḥaqquq). It was also read as futtiḥat (فُتِّحَتْ) with the doubled tā' (tashdīd), and this is the more suitable reading in light of His words: ﴿so it will be gates﴾, meaning its opened gates became many, because of the descent of the angels in an unusual descent, until it became as though it were nothing but opened gates (p-90), like His words: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾, as though all of it were gushing springs. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with clouds﴾, which is the cloud mentioned in His words: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud, with the angels?﴾, i.e., His command and His punishment. It was said that "al-abwab" means the roads and paths, i.e., it will be stripped away, its place will become open, and it will become passages that nothing blocks.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 20:**

﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾, that is, they will move through the air in their own forms after being uprooted from their places, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass as the passing of clouds﴾. That is, you see them with your own eyes as still in their places, while in fact they pass like clouds driven by the winds at a swift pace. This is because great bodies, when they move in any direction, hardly show their motion, even when moving very fast, especially from a distance. To this refers the saying of the one who said:

*With a host as vast as a mountain, you think they are standing still for a pilgrim, while the riding camels amble along.*

Within this comparison is included a comparison of the state of the mountains with the state of the clouds in the loosening of their parts and their scattering, as His saying, exalted is He, speaks of it: ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of wool, fluffed up﴾. God, exalted is He, will change the earth and alter its form, and will set the mountains in motion in that terrifying form when creatures are gathered after the second blast, so that they may witness them. Then He will scatter them in the air. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will become dust scattered﴾, that is, after being set in motion they will become like a mirage (*sarab*), as in His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust﴾ ﴿and they will become scattered dust﴾, that is, dust dispersed. Although they will be leveled and split apart at the first blast, their motion and the leveling of the earth will occur only after the second blast, as His saying, exalted is He, speaks of it: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains; say, My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾ ﴿and He will leave it a level plain﴾ ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or curvature﴾ ﴿on that Day they will follow the caller﴾. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the earth will be changed into another earth, and the heavens too, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer﴾. For the following of the caller, who is Israfil, peace be upon him, and the coming forth of creation before God, exalted is He, occur only after the second blast.

Verse 21: ﴿Indeed, Hell has always been a place of lying in ambush.﴾

This begins the detailed statement of the rulings of the Decisive Judgment (al-fasl), to which "the Day" has been attributed, following a clarification that is due to it. The reason for presenting the description of the state of the disbelievers first is in no need of explanation.

Al-mirsad (a place of ambush) is a noun for the place where one lies in wait, like al-midmar (the training ground), which is the noun for the place where horses are trained (addamar), and al-minhaj (the road), which is the noun for the place where one travels (yanhaj). That is to say: Hell was, by the judgment and decree of Allah the Exalted, a place of ambush, in which the guardians of the Fire lie in wait for the disbelievers in order to punish them therein.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 22:

﴿لِلطّاغِينَ﴾ is related to an implied verb, and it is either an attributive modifier (na't) of "mirsadan" (ambush/watchpost), meaning: existing for the tyrants (lil-taghin). The Exalted's statement:

"maaban" (a place of return)

is a substitute (badal) for it, meaning: a place of return to which they will certainly return. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of "maaban," placed before it because it is indefinite (nakira); had it been placed after it, it would have been a descriptive modifier (sifa) of it. It has also been permitted that it be related to "maaban" itself, so that the meaning is: it is an ambush for both groups, a place of return for the disbelievers in particular; but its remoteness is not hidden, for what is immediately understood from it being an ambush for one group is that they are being punished by it. It has been said: it is an ambush for the people of Paradise, whom the angels watch over, who receive them there, because their passing (majaz) over it is toward it, and it is a place of return for the tyrants. (p-91) It has also been said: al-mirsad is an intensive form (sighat mubalagha) from al-rasd (watching), and the meaning is: it is intently watching the disbelievers so that not one of them escapes. It was also read with the fath (inna with a fatha), on the basis that the establishment of the Hour is explained by its being an ambush for the tyrants.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 23:

﴿Lābithīna fīhā﴾ [remaining therein] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara, a future-anticipated state) from the pronoun hidden in "lil-ṭāghīna" [for the transgressors]. It is also read as (Labithīna). The Exalted's statement ﴿aḥqāban﴾ [for ages] is an adverb of time (ẓarf) for their staying, meaning: ages in succession, such that whenever one age (ḥuqb) passes, another ḥuqb follows it, without end. The word ḥuqb is hardly used except where the succession and continuation of times is intended, so there is nothing in it indicating that those ages have a limit. Even if ḥuqb were taken to mean eighty years, or seventy thousand years, [the point stands]. The Exalted's statement:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verses 24–25:

﴿They shall not taste therein any coolness, nor any drink,﴾ ﴿except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid.﴾

This is a independent nominal clause (jumlah mubtada'ah), informing about them that they shall not taste therein anything at all of coolness or refreshment that would cool down for them the heat of the Fire, nor any drink that would quench their thirst; rather, they shall taste therein boiling water (hamim) and dark, pus-like liquid (ghassaq).

It is also said: "al-barad" (coolness) means sleep. And it has been recited as "ghassaqan" with the lightened form (taskhif). Both (ghassaq and its variant) refer to what flows from their pus (sadid).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verses 24–25:

﴿They shall not taste therein any coolness, nor any drink,﴾ ﴿except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid.﴾

This is a independent nominal clause (jumlah mubtada'ah), informing about them that they shall not taste therein anything at all of coolness or refreshment that would cool down for them the heat of the Fire, nor any drink that would quench their thirst; rather, they shall taste therein boiling water (hamim) and dark, pus-like liquid (ghassaq).

It is also said: "al-barad" (coolness) means sleep. And it has been recited as "ghassaqan" with the lightened form (taskhif). Both (ghassaq and its variant) refer to what flows from their pus (sadid).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 26:

﴿Jazaa'an﴾ means: recompense them with this as a recompense (jaza'an).

﴿Wifaqan﴾ means: corresponding to their deeds, or the very correspondence (wifaq) for the sake of emphasis, or it corresponds to them as a correspondence (wifaqan). It is also read (Wafaqan), as a form of the verb waafaqa (to agree with, to match), meaning: it befits them, i.e., it suits them (laqahu).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, they used not to expect a reckoning﴾ This is a causal explanation for their deserving the recompense mentioned, that is: they used not to fear that they would be called to account for their deeds.

﴿And they denied Our signs﴾, which clearly state this.

﴿Denying intensely﴾, i.e., denial in an excessive degree; and for this reason they persisted in disbelief and in various kinds of sin. The form "fi'al" from the pattern "fa'ala" (the intensive form, Form II) is common among eloquent speakers. It has also been read with lightening (kadhdhaban → kadhaban), in which case it is a verbal noun (masdar) of "kadhdhaba", as in the verse of the poet:

*Fasadaqtuha wa-kadhabtuha, wal-mar'u yanfa'uhu kidhabuhu*
("So I told her the truth and I lied to her, and a man benefits from his lying.")

Its accusative case (intisab) is either due to a verb implied by "kadhdhabu" (i.e., "And they denied Our signs, so they denied with denial"), or due to "kadhdhabu" itself, since it implies the meaning of "kadhdhabu" [in the sense of "they lied"], for everyone who denies the truth is a liar. It has also been read as "kuzzaban", which is the plural of "kadhib" (liar), in which case its accusative is in the circumstantial (hal) sense: "they denied Our signs being liars." Also, "kaddhdhab" may mean the single person who is eloquent in lying, and so it is made an adjective of the verbal noun of "kadhdhabu": i.e., a denial of intense lying, excessive in its falsehood.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 29:

﴿And everything﴾ — that is, of the things of which their deeds are a part — and its being in the accusative is by a hidden verb that is explained by ﴿We have counted it﴾, i.e., We have preserved it and kept account of it. It is also read in the nominative (marfu') by way of inception (al-ibtida'), ﴿a Book﴾ — a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing ﴿We have counted it﴾, because counting (al-ihsa') and writing (al-kataba) are of one kind; or it is in apposition to its implied verb; or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) meaning ﴿written﴾ in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), or in the scrolls of the recording angels (suhuf al-hafaza), and the clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 30:

﴿So taste [it], for We shall not increase you except in punishment.﴾ This is a consequence of their disbelief in the Reckoning and their denial of the signs. The shift from the third person to the second person, which indicates the intensification of the threat, and the use of "lan" (never), which conveys that the non-increase [of punishment] is among the things that do not admit of being true, indicate the extreme of anger, which is not hidden. The Prophet (ﷺ) has also related: ﴿that this verse is the most severe in the Qur'an for the people of the Fire﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 31:

﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing there is an attainment (mafaz).﴾ This begins the explanation of the praiseworthy states of the believers, following the explanation of the wretched states of the disbelievers. That is: indeed, for those who guard themselves against disbelief and the rest of the vile deeds of the disbelievers, there is success (fawz) and triumph in attaining their desires; or it is a place of success. It has also been said: (it means) deliverance from what those (disbelievers) are in; or it is a place of deliverance. And His, exalted is He, saying:
Gardens and grapevines: that is, orchards containing all kinds of fruit-bearing trees, and vineyards. It is in apposition (badal) to "mafazan" (a place of triumph).

"And maidens with swelling breasts" (Qur'an 78:33): that is, women whose breasts have become firm and rounded, and they are the nawahid (maidens with firm, upright breasts). "Of equal age" (atraban): that is, of the same age (lidat).
And a full cup (kasan dihaqa). That is: a brimming cup. It is said: "adhaqa al-hawd" means he filled the basin.

They hear therein (i.e., in Paradise); it is also said: in the cup.

Neither vain talk nor lying. That is, they do not utter vain talk, and some of them do not call others liars. It is also recited as (kiddaban) with the short vowel, meaning: he does not deny him, or he does not lie to him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 36:

﴿As a recompense from your Lord﴾ is a emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) in the accusative, governed by the sense of "Indeed for the God-fearing there is an attainment (mafaz)", for it has the force of saying: "He recompensed the God-fearing with an attainment, as a recompense existing from your Lord." The mention of the title of Lordship (al-rububiyyah), which indicates the gradual perfection of the bestowal, together with its being attributed to His pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, is an added honouring of him (ﷺ).

﴿A gift﴾ means: a bounty and a benefaction from Him, exalted is He, since nothing is obligatory upon Him. It is a substitute (badal) for "recompense".

﴿Sufficient (hisaban)﴾ is an attribute of "gift", in the sense of: sufficient, on the basis of a verbal noun that has been placed in the position of an adjective, or it has been intensified from (ahsabahu al-shay'), when the thing suffices him, to the point that one says "hasbi (sufficient for me)". It is said: "according to their deeds." And it has been read as (hissaban) with the doubling of the letter sin, on the basis that it means the one who reckons, like "al-dirak" meaning "the one who overtakes".

(p-93) ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for "رَبِّكَ" (*rabbika*, "your Lord"). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ (*al-Rahman*), is a *sifah* (attribute, qualifier) of Him. It has also been said that it is an attribute of the first noun. Either way, mentioning His lordship over all things and His vast mercy indicates the basis on which the mentioned recompense rests. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they will not have the power to address Him﴾ (*yamlikuna minhu khitaban*) is an *isti'naf* (resumptive, new sentence) that confirms what the general lordship conveys of utmost greatness and majesty, and His independence in the mentioned recompense and bounty, without anyone having power over it.

It was read as *rafʿihima* (both in the nominative). It has been said that the two are predicates of an omitted subject (*mubtada'* mudmar, an implied subject). It has been said that the second is an adjective (*na't*) of the first. It has been said that the first is the subject (*mubtada'*) and the second is its predicate, and "لا يَمْلِكُونَ" (*la yamlikuna*, "they do not have the power") is another predicate. Or it is the predicate, and "الرَّحْمَنُ" (*al-Rahman*) is an attribute of the first. It has been said that "لا يَمْلِكُونَ" is a permanent circumstantial clause (*hal lazimah*). It has also been said that the first is a subject, "الرَّحْمَنُ" is a second subject, and "يَمْلِكُونُ" (*yamlikuna*) is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the first. The linkage is achieved by repeating the subject with its meaning, according to the view of those who hold this. The most appropriate reading is that both are nominative by way of praise (*al-madh*), or that the second is an attribute of the first and "لا يَمْلِكُونَ" is a resumptive sentence as it stands. In that case it contains what was mentioned of the indication of the basis of recompense and bounty, as in the apposition, because the nominative or accusative of praise follows what precedes it in meaning, even if it is grammatically disjoined from it, as was explained in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

It was read as *jarr al-awwal* (the first in the genitive) by apposition, with the second in the nominative as a *mubtada'* whose predicate is what follows it. Or it is a predicate of an omitted subject, and what follows is a resumptive sentence. Or it is a second predicate, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The pronoun in "لا يَمْلِكُونَ" refers to the people of the heavens and the earth, meaning: they do not have the power to address Him, exalted is He, on their own initiative, as the word "الْمَلِكِ" (*al-Malik*, "the King") indicates, *khitaban ma fi shay'in ma* (an address concerning anything at all). The intended meaning is the negation of their power to address Him, exalted is He, with anything concerning a reduction of punishment or an increase of reward without His permission, in the most emphatic and strongest form. It has also been said: they do not have in their hands any address from God, concerning what He commands in matters of reward and punishment, that they could dispose of as owners do, so as to add to it or subtract from it.

﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾. It is said: the Spirit is a creation greater than the angels, nobler than them, and closer to the Lord of the worlds. It is also said: it is an angel, and God, Mighty and Majestic, has created nothing greater than it after the Throne.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when the Day of Resurrection comes, he (the Spirit) will stand alone in a row, and all the angels will stand in a row. From him, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: ﴿The Spirit is one of the soldiers of Allah, the Exalted. They are not angels. They have heads, hands and feet, and they eat food.﴾ Then he recited, "On the Day when the Spirit stands," to the end of the verse.

This is also the view of Abu Salih and Mujahid, who said: No angel descends from the heaven without being accompanied by one of them. This is transmitted by al-Baghawi. It is also said: they are the noblest of the angels. It is said: they are guardians over the angels. It is said: it is Jibril (peace be upon him).

"Saffan" (صَفًّا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a grammatical state describing the subject at the time of the action), meaning "arranged in rows." It is said: they are two rows, the Spirit forming one row and the angels another, or the Spirit being multiple and the angels one row. It is said: "ṣuffūf" (صُفُوف) means the horizon, based on His saying, ﴿and the angel in rows upon rows﴾. It is also said: all of them stand in one row.

"Yawm" (يَوْمَ) is an adverb of time (ẓarf) governing His saying, ﴿they will not speak﴾. His saying, ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and who says what is right﴾, is a substitute (badal, a noun that replaces an earlier one) for the pronoun in "they will not speak," which refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, of whom the Spirit and the angels are part. He mentioned their standing and their arrangement in rows to establish the greatness of His dominion and the majesty of His lordship, and to make dreadful the Day of Resurrection, on which the whole discourse of the noble surah turns from its beginning to its end.

This sentence is a resumptive clause (istinā', a new sentence that continues the discourse) that confirms the meaning of His saying, ﴿they do not possess﴾ ... etc., and emphasizes it: that the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, if on that day they cannot speak about anything of the kind of speech except one whom Allah the Exalted has permitted among them to speak, and that permitted one says what is right, meaning what is true, then how could they possess the power to address the Lord of Might? This is so even though address is more specific than speech in general and more exalted in its aim. It does not mean that the Spirit and the angels, despite being the most excellent of creation and the closest of them to Allah the Exalted, cannot speak what is right of intercession for whomever He approves except with His permission; so how could anyone else speak to Him?

As it is said, this reading is founded on the principle of i'tizal (the Mu'tazilite school of rational theology), so whoever follows it while permitting "yawm" to be an adverb governing "they do not possess" has confused the matters and mixed his thoughts with doubts.

It is also said: "illā man adhina..." (إلّا مَن أذِنَ) to the end is in the accusative as an exception in its basic sense. The meaning is: they will not speak except concerning a person whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and that person says what is right, meaning the truth, which is monotheism. The divine name "al-Raḥmān" (the Most Merciful) is placed where a pronoun would be expected, to indicate that the basis of the permission is extreme mercy, and not that anyone deserves it from Him, glorified and exalted is He.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the Day of their standing in the manner mentioned. The sense of distance in it, along with the nearness of the time of the thing referred to, serves to signal the elevation of its rank and the remoteness of its station in terror and magnificence. Its grammatical position is nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is what follows it, meaning: that is the Great Day on which the Spirit and the angels will stand in ranks, neither they nor others being able to speak out of awe and majesty.

﴿The Day of Truth﴾, that is, the one that is established and certain without doubt, with no diverting force to turn it aside and no inclining power to bend it back. The fa' in His words, ﴿So whoever wills, let him take to his Lord a place of return﴾, is a fa' faṣīḥah (an eloquent fa', which indicates an omitted condition). The object of "wills" is omitted because the clause falls as a conditional, because its object is what the consequence guarantees, and because its attachment to it is not strange according to the established rule. "To his Lord" is connected to "a place of return," and was placed before it for emphasis and to preserve the rhyme of the verse endings. It is as if it were said: Since the matter is as mentioned, namely that the aforementioned Day is certain without doubt, whoever wills to take as his return the reward of his Lord, whose great majesty has been mentioned, let him do so through faith and obedience. Qatadah said: "a place of return" means a way. The attachment of the preposition is because it carries the sense of leading to and reaching, as has passed in His words: ﴿for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 78, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, We have warned you﴾ That is: by what was mentioned in the surah of the verses that speak of resurrection (al-ba'th) and of what follows it of calamities (al-dawahi). Or: by them, and by all the calamities (al-qawari'), revealed in the Qur'an.

﴿a near punishment﴾ It is the punishment of the Hereafter, and its nearness is for the certainty of its coming as a decree. It is also near in relation to Him, exalted is He, even if they see it as far away, and they will see it as near, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾.

And from Qatada: it is the punishment of this world, because it is the nearer of the two punishments. And from Muqatil: it is the killing of the Quraysh on the Day of Badr. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿on the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾, it is either a substitute (badal) for "a punishment," or an adverbial phrase (zarf) for a hidden verb that is a description of it, meaning: a punishment occurring on the day when a man looks, that is, sees (yushahid) what he sent forward of good or evil. This is on the basis that "ma" is a relative pronoun in the accusative governed by "yanzuru," with a omitted returning pronoun. Or: he looks at whatever his hands have sent forth, on the basis that it is an interrogative in the accusative governed by "qaddamat." It has been said: "al-mar'" is an expression for the disbeliever. The "ma" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!"﴾ is apparent, placed in the position of the pronoun to increase the blame. It has been said: the meaning of his wish, "Would that I were dust," is: in the world, so that I would not have been created and would not have been made responsible; or: "Would that I were dust on this day, so that I would not be resurrected." It has also been said: God, exalted is He, will gather the animals and will carry out retribution for the hornless (jamma') against the horned (qarna'), then He will return them to dust, so the disbeliever will wish his state were theirs. It has also been said: the disbeliever is Iblis, who sees Adam and his offspring and their reward, so he wishes he were the thing he despised when he said: "You created me from fire and created him from clay."

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah 'Amma yatasa'aluna, God will give him to drink the cool of drink on the Day of Resurrection, and praise be to God alone."
